title: OpenAI starts alpha-testing Private Inference, sealing enterprise prompts inside hardware enclaves
subtitle: Sam Altman announced the limited rollout on X on November 25, two months after the feature was previewed at DevDay and with pricing, hardware and supported models still undisclosed.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Sam Altman posted on X on November 25 that OpenAI has started alpha-testing Private Inference with a small group of business customers. The feature runs inference inside confidential-computing enclaves — hardware-isolated regions of a server where prompts and responses stay encrypted while the model processes them, so that neither OpenAI operators nor co-tenants can read what the customer sent. Altman's post directed interested organizations to an OpenAI employee leading the effort, who said in follow-up replies that OpenAI is acquiring more confidential-computing capacity to widen the rollout.

Private Inference first appeared at DevDay on September 29 as part of a broader Private Intelligence package that also includes zero data retention and an optional enterprise key-management layer. The November 25 move is the first time OpenAI has put any of it into customer hands. The alpha carries no published price, no list of supported models or endpoints, and no public attestation report — the cryptographic proof that a given workload ran inside a sealed enclave rather than an ordinary VM. OpenAI has not said whether coverage extends to ChatGPT Enterprise and Codex or stays on the API alone.

Confidential computing on the inference path is where the last two years of enterprise AI contracting has been pushing. Banks and hospitals have been slow to send regulated data to a cloud model that logs prompts for abuse monitoring, and every major hyperscaler has shipped TEE-backed VM options for bring-your-own-model workloads. Putting the frontier labs' own hosted models behind the same guarantee removes one of the last structural reasons a Fortune 500 customer defers to on-prem or smaller vendors — and it costs OpenAI something, because enclaves carry a meaningful compute premium over a plain H100 or TPU slot.

A note for learners: when a vendor says a feature is private, ask what the attestation is and who signs it. Private Inference will mean something only when a customer can verify — cryptographically, through a chain they trust — that a specific prompt ran inside a specific enclave on a specific chip, with a specific model binary, and nothing was copied out. Everything short of that is a trust statement, not a security property.
